body.text: Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae and Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke for more than 30 minutes while standing in Shenzhen, China, on November 18, shortly after a welcome dinner for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, according to the Japanese government.
It was the first face-to-face exchange between Japanese and Russian leaders since Abe Shinzo met Putin in September 2019, and the first since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The talks came just one day after two aircraft believed to be Russian violated Japanese airspace off Fukuoka Prefecture.
The discussion took place with the agreement of both sides, Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara Minoru said on November 19.
Kihara confirmed that Takaichi raised the detention of Hokkaido Shimbun journalist Imai Yuki and issues involving the protection of Japanese companies in Russia.
Asked whether Takaichi had called for Imai’s immediate release, Kihara said only that she had discussed the matter with Putin based on Japan’s position.
The two leaders agreed to keep talking at various levels.
At a press conference in Shenzhen on November 19, Takaichi said, “The biggest progress was that President Putin and I were able to create an environment where we can communicate directly.”

Kihara declined to say whether Takaichi had also protested Putin’s August visit to Iturup Island (known in Japan as Etorofu) or the November 17 airspace violation, citing the need to keep diplomatic talks private.
However, Japan’s Mainichi Shimbun reported on November 19 that Takaichi was believed to have raised concerns about both Japan Tobacco’s business in Russia and the airspace violation.
According to Japan’s Ministry of Defense, two aircraft believed to be Russian violated Japanese airspace northwest of Okinoshima Island, off Fukuoka Prefecture, early on November 17.
The first aircraft entered at about 4:07 a.m. and left at about 4:10 a.m. The second entered at about 4:09 a.m. and left three minutes later.
Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighter jets and issued repeated radio warnings.
At a press conference that day, I asked Air Self-Defense Force Chief of Staff General Morita Takehiro what type of aircraft had entered Japanese airspace.
“At this stage, we have not been able to identify the aircraft,” he replied, adding that their Russian origin remained an estimate.

Morita said this was the seventh airspace violation by Russian aircraft near the Tsushima Strait, including cases during the Soviet era. In 2013, two Russian Tu-95 strategic bombers violated Japanese airspace near Okinoshima.

After passing through the Tsushima Strait, the two aircraft flew between Taiwan and the Okinawa island of Yonaguni, Japan’s westernmost island, before reaching the Pacific Ocean. According to Japan’s Joint Staff Office, this was only the second time Russian aircraft had reached the Pacific via this route, following a similar flight in January 2010.
South Korea’s military reported that several Russian military aircraft entered its air defense identification zone (ADIZ) over the Sea of Japan (also known as the East Sea) on November 17.
Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense also reported that two Russian military aircraft entered its ADIZ from the northeast, flew east of Taiwan, and left south of Taitung on the same day.
Entering an ADIZ does not itself mean violating national airspace.

Meanwhile, The War Zone reported that two Russian Tu-95MS bombers and two support aircraft arrived in Da Nang, Vietnam, on November 17. It remains unclear whether the aircraft reported by South Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam were the same aircraft that violated Japanese airspace.
The airspace violation came just before Putin’s arrival in Shenzhen for talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and other world leaders.

One possible reading is that the flights were meant as a “gift” from Putin to Xi, showing Russia’s support for China at a time of growing tensions between Beijing and both Tokyo and Taipei. Russia and China have built closer military ties in recent years, including through joint exercises and long-range bomber flights.
The flight route near Taiwan was also striking. China-Japan relations have worsened since Takaichi’s remarks on a possible Taiwan conflict in November 2025.

In Shenzhen, Xi and Takaichi shook hands before the welcome dinner, but no formal China-Japan summit was held. Takaichi later said she had thanked Xi and congratulated him on hosting the APEC meetings.
Still, there is no public evidence that Moscow and Beijing planned the flights together or that they were ordered by Putin to send a message to Xi.

Japan-Russia ties have taken a turn for the worse in the past three months. In August, Putin visited Iturup, the largest of the four Russian-held islands that Japan claims as its Northern Territories. In October, Russian authorities detained Japanese journalists Imai on suspicion of spying. In November, Putin signed orders placing Japan Tobacco’s Russian companies under temporary Russian management, eventually covering seven local companies.

Despite these disputes, Tokyo has kept diplomatic channels open. On October 30, Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu met Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in the first face-to-face meeting between the two countries’ foreign ministers in five years.
Japan has also kept its sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine, while Moscow has criticized Tokyo’s policies as unfriendly.
The next test will be whether the renewed talks help secure Imai’s release and address the problems facing Japan Tobacco in Russia.
